title: Strings: Mutability, Indexing, and Memory Behavior
description: How strings differ in mutability, indexing/slicing, available methods, and underlying memory representation.
objectives: Compare string mutability across the three languages

content.heading: Python
content.body: str is immutable — every transformation (replace, upper, etc.) returns a new string. Indexing (text[0]) and rich slicing (text[1:4], text[::-1]) are both built in, with negative indices supported. A large, built-in set of methods (split, join, strip, format, ...) covers most common needs directly, with no separate import required.

content.heading: Java
content.body: String is immutable, exactly like Python's str — every 'modifying' method returns a new String. Indexing uses a method, charAt(i), not bracket syntax (Java has no [] operator overloading for arbitrary types); there's no negative indexing or slice syntax — substring(begin, end) covers slicing but with a more verbose call. For frequent concatenation, StringBuilder provides a genuinely mutable buffer, working around String's immutability performance cost.

content.heading: C
content.body: A 'string' is just a mutable char array with a null terminator — there's no distinct string type, so mutability is unrestricted (and unmanaged) at the language level: individual characters can be directly assigned (str[0] = 'X';), unlike Python's or Java's immutable strings. Indexing uses array syntax (str[i]), but there's no slicing at all — extracting a substring requires manual copying with strncpy or similar. Memory is the programmer's full responsibility: buffer sizing, the null terminator, and any resizing must all be handled manually.

content.heading: Key Differences
content.body: Python's str and Java's String are both immutable, safe, garbage-collected objects with rich built-in support; C's strings are raw, mutable, manually-managed char arrays with essentially no built-in safety. Python's slicing syntax has no equivalent in Java (which needs substring() calls) or C (which needs manual buffer manipulation).

content.heading: When It Matters
content.body: String-heavy code ported from Python to C requires the most rework by far, since virtually none of Python's convenient string operations (slicing, rich methods, automatic memory management) exist natively in C — they must be reimplemented, carefully, with explicit buffer size management.

keyPoints: Python's str and Java's String are both immutable and memory-managed automatically; C strings are mutable, raw char arrays managed manually
Python supports rich slicing (text[1:4]); Java requires substring() calls; C requires manual buffer copying
C string handling carries real safety risks (buffer overflows) that simply don't exist in Python or Java
